Evidence-based data to recommend either for or against the use of ivermectin are needed. OBJECTIVE: To determine the efficacy of ivermectin in preventing progression to severe disease among high-risk patients with COVID-19. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: The Ivermectin Treatment Efficacy in COVID-19 High-Risk Patients (I-TECH) study was an open-label randomized clinical trial conducted at 20 public hospitals and a COVID-19 quarantine center in Malaysia between May 31 and October 25, 2021. Within the first week of patients' symptom onset, the study enrolled patients 50 years and older with laboratory-confirmed COVID-19, comorbidities, and mild to moderate disease. INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive either oral ivermectin, 0.4 mg/kg body weight daily for 5 days, plus standard of care (n = 241) or standard of care alone (n = 249). The standard of care consisted of symptomatic therapy and monitoring for signs of early deterioration based on clinical findings, laboratory test results, and chest imaging. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was the proportion of patients who progressed to severe disease, defined as the hypoxic stage requiring supplemental oxygen to maintain pulse oximetry oxygen saturation of 95% or higher. Secondary outcomes of the trial included the rates of mechanical ventilation, intensive care unit admission, 28-day in-hospital mortality, and adverse events. RESULTS: Among 490 patients included in the primary analysis (mean [SD] age, 62.5 [8.7] years; 267 women [54.5%]), 52 of 241 patients (21.6%) in the ivermectin group and 43 of 249 patients (17.3%) in the control group progressed to severe disease (relative risk [RR], 1.25; 95% CI, 0.87-1.80; P = .25). For all prespecified secondary outcomes, there were no significant differences between groups. Mechanical ventilation occurred in 4 (1.7%) vs 10 (4.0%) (RR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.13-1.30; P = .17), intensive care unit admission in 6 (2.4%) vs 8 (3.2%) (RR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.27-2.20; P = .79), and 28-day in-hospital death in 3 (1.2%) vs 10 (4.0%) (RR, 0.31; 95% CI, 0.09-1.11; P = .09). The most common adverse event reported was diarrhea (14 [5.8%] in the ivermectin group and 4 [1.6%] in the control group). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this randomized clinical trial of high-risk patients with mild to moderate COVID-19, ivermectin treatment during early illness did not prevent progression to severe disease. The study findings do not support the use of ivermectin for patients with COVID-19. text:
**Ivermectin for treating COVID-19: what the trials show**

The best evidence says ivermectin does not work for COVID-19. Large, well-run, placebo-controlled trials found no meaningful effect on hospitalisation, death, getting worse or time to recovery. Some early meta-analyses did report large benefits. That signal faded once lower-quality, unregistered and possibly fraudulent trials were removed. That pattern is a good case study for your methods course.

## 1. Key randomised trials

| Trial | Setting / N | Dose | Main result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TOGETHER** (Brazil) [W4220754707] | High-risk outpatients; 679 ivermectin vs 679 placebo | 400 µg/kg × 3 days | Hospitalisation or long ER stay: 14.7% vs 16.3%, RR 0.90 (95% CrI 0.70–1.16). No effect on secondary outcomes. |
| **ACTIV-6**, 400 µg/kg (US) [W4307043809] | Outpatients; 817 vs 774 | 400 µg/kg × 3 days | Time to recovery HR 1.07 (0.96–1.17). Hospitalisation or death 1.2% in both arms. |
| **ACTIV-6**, 600 µg/kg (US) [W4312115096] *(preprint)* | Outpatients; 602 vs 604; 84% vaccinated | Up to 600 µg/kg × 6 days | Time to recovery HR 1.02 (0.92–1.13). Hospitalisation, death or urgent care 5.7% vs 6.0%. |
| **COVID-OUT** (US) [W4292148078] | Outpatients with overweight or obesity; 1,323 analysed (2×3 factorial design) | — | Primary composite (low oxygen, ER visit, hospitalisation or death): aOR 1.05 (0.76–1.45). |
| **PRINCIPLE** (UK) [W4392303143] | Community; 2,157 ivermectin vs 3,256 usual care; open-label | 300–400 µg/kg × 3 days | Recovery about 2 days faster (HR 1.15, 1.07–1.23), but only a 19% chance of reaching the pre-set "meaningful" threshold. Hospitalisation or death OR 1.02 (0.63–1.62). No benefit at 3, 6 or 12 months. |
| **I-TECH** (Malaysia) [W4212973150] | Patients ≥50 with other conditions; 490; open-label | 400 µg/kg × 5 days | Progression to severe disease: 21.6% vs 17.3%, RR 1.25 (0.87–1.80). Death RR 0.31 (0.09–1.11), not significant. |
| **López-Medina** (Colombia) [W3135420706] | Mild disease; 400 | 300 µg/kg × 5 days | Time to symptom resolution HR 1.07 (0.87–1.32). |

Things to notice:
- **Consistent nulls.** The results agree across countries, doses up to 600 µg/kg, vaccinated and unvaccinated groups, and double-blind and open-label designs.
- **Doses were adequate.** "Wrong dose" is a common objection, but these trials used doses well above the standard antiparasitic dose.
- **Read PRINCIPLE carefully.** It was open-label and its recovery outcome was self-reported, so lack of blinding could explain the small benefit it found. The blinded trials (ACTIV-6, López-Medina) found no difference.

Many smaller trials also turned up (e.g. [W4283363264], [W4377292376], [W3111068209], [W4212946211], [W4311938754]). Screen and assess each one formally; I haven't extracted them all.

## 2. Systematic reviews: how trial quality changed the answer

- **Bryant et al. 2021** [W3168908540] pooled 24 trials and reported a large drop in deaths (RR 0.38, 0.19–0.73), rated "moderate certainty".
- **Hill et al. 2021** [W3121596699] found a similar benefit. **It was retracted** [10.1093/ofid/ofac056]. In a follow-up, the same authors split trials by quality [W4206432189]. The suspected fraudulent trial showed RR 0.08, while low-risk trials showed RR 0.96 (0.56–1.66). In their words, the survival benefit "was dependent on largely poor-quality studies."
- **Roman et al. 2021** [W3174188666] found no significant effect on deaths (RR 0.37, 0.12–1.13; very low certainty). Only the 3 high-risk-of-bias trials showed a reduction.
- **Cochrane 2022** [W4283205481] is probably your best anchor. It only accepted trials registered in advance, which removed 7 of the 14 trials from its previous version, and parked 28 trials as "awaiting classification" because of problems in their reporting. For outpatients, ivermectin probably has little or no effect on deaths (RR 0.77, 0.47–1.25; moderate certainty). For inpatients the evidence is very uncertain. It found no usable prevention trials.

## 3. Retractions to check for

- The Hill meta-analysis [10.1093/ofid/ofac056].
- The Pott-Junior pilot trial, *Toxicology Reports* [10.1016/j.toxrep.2022.04.009, original W3134585354].
- The IRICT trial, *Expert Review of Anti-infective Therapy*, retracted in 2024 [10.1080/14787210.2024.2362097, original W4283838215].

The database lists the original papers with no retraction flag, and the notices have no text, so I can't tell you why each was retracted. Check every included study against the Retraction Watch database.

The trial behind the Hill retraction is widely reported to be the Elgazzar preprint, but it isn't in this database, so check that yourself. Several prevention meta-analyses (e.g. [W4313209660], [W4309361513]) and a large observational prevention study [W4206412576] also exist. Cochrane found no eligible prevention RCTs, so treat those with caution.

## 4. Suggestions for your review
1. Set integrity checks before you search: require trial registration in advance and check for retractions. Cochrane's approach is a good model to cite.
2. Analyse results by risk of bias. The way the effect shrinks in better trials is your central finding.
3. Analyse outpatients and inpatients separately, and keep treatment separate from prevention.
4. Keep blinded and open-label trials apart when the outcome is self-reported, like time to recovery.
5. Rate certainty with GRADE. Bryant and Cochrane reached opposite "moderate certainty" conclusions, which is a good discussion point.

**Bottom line:** the most reliable trials (TOGETHER, ACTIV-6 at two doses, COVID-OUT, PRINCIPLE, I-TECH) consistently show no clinically meaningful benefit of ivermectin for COVID-19. The early positive meta-analyses depended on low-quality and possibly fraudulent studies.

I should have given you my criteria. Only randomized controlled trials of oral or intravenous ivermectin in people with confirmed or suspected COVID-19, compared with placebo, no treatment, standard care or another drug. No prophylaxis trials in people without COVID-19, no observational studies, no lab or animal studies, and no reviews. Please give me the full updated list of included trials.

{"id": "W4321366419", "doi": "10.7554/elife.83201", "title": "Pharmacometrics of high-dose ivermectin in early COVID-19 from an open label, randomized, controlled adaptive platform trial (PLATCOV)", "abstract": "BACKGROUND: There is no generally accepted methodology for in vivo assessment of antiviral activity in SARS-CoV-2 infections. METHODS: In a multicentre open label, randomized, controlled adaptive platform trial, adult patients with early symptomatic COVID-19 were randomized to one of six treatment arms including high-dose oral ivermectin (600 µg/kg daily for 7 days), the monoclonal antibodies casirivimab and imdevimab (600 mg/600 mg), and no study drug. This was derived from daily log10 viral densities in standardized duplicate oropharyngeal swab eluates. This ongoing trial is registered at https://clinicaltrials.gov/ (NCT05041907). RESULTS: Randomization to the ivermectin arm was stopped after enrolling 205 patients into all arms, as the prespecified futility threshold was reached. CONCLUSIONS: High-dose ivermectin did not have measurable antiviral activity in early symptomatic COVID-19. ## B. Needs your decision: ivermectin given with a drug the control group didn't get
These trials technically match your wording, but they can't isolate ivermectin's effect. Cochrane's rule is that co-interventions must be the same in both arms [W4283205481]. I'd suggest adding that rule and excluding these:
- Mahmud, Bangladesh: ivermectin + doxycycline vs placebo [W3162891398]
- Hashim, Iraq: ivermectin + doxycycline vs standard care [W4287129885]
- Chowdhury: ivermectin + doxycycline vs HCQ + azithromycin [W3133633583]
- Exman, Brazil, cancer patients: losartan + ivermectin vs placebo [W4396610082]
- FINCOV, Thailand: favipiravir/ivermectin/niclosamide vs favipiravir; registered only after the trial was done [W4393320918]
- Babalola, Nigeria: ivermectin alone vs HCQ + ivermectin + azithromycin [W4243260355]. Both arms got ivermectin, so I'd exclude this one under any rule.

## E. Excluded, with reasons
- **No randomisation described:** Rahman, Bangladesh [W3046318930], which just says patients were "divided into two groups". Check the full text.
- **Observational:** IDEA protocol [W3085858594], Rajter [W3091860795], [W4386597728], [W4378516419], [W3217293035], [W3102430453], [W4206412576], a case series [W3046413061], and a cross-sectional study [W3161928646].
- **Not oral or IV:** nasal spray [W3168400794].
- **Prevention in people without COVID-19:** [W3129600723], [W3143180683], [W3100710042]. The PCR-negative group of [W4282595092] is also excluded.

I opened all 10 records. **7 are included and 3 are excluded.** One of the excluded papers raises an integrity issue you should record.

## Section 15 papers (previously not assessed)

| Paper | Decision | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Rani et al., "Role of Ivermectin in the Treatment of COVID 19", *Int J Adv Res* 2021 [W3213437465] | **Exclude** | **Not an independent trial.** Its results match Ahmed et al. 2020 [W3107056972] word for word: "9.7 days vs 12.7 days p = 0.02… ivermectin Plus doxycycline arm (11.5 days p = 0.27)". It has different authors, gives no methods, setting or sample size, and lists only one reference. It is either a summary of Ahmed's trial or reuses its data without credit. Count the trial once (as Ahmed), and note the exclusion reason as "duplicate data, not original trial; possible plagiarism". |
| Helaly et al., "Role of Ivermectin in Management of COVID-19", 2022 [W4220764004] | **Exclude** | Narrative review, not a trial. |
| Sekhon, "Repurposing Drugs for Covid-19 by a Developing Country", 2022 [W4289979425] | **Exclude** | Observational cohort with no randomisation or control group: 415 patients in Honduras given a combination of ivermectin, aspirin, colchicine, fluvoxamine and famotidine. It would also fail the same-other-treatments rule. |

## The seven trials not yet checked

| Trial | Decision | Design and setting | Main findings |
|---|---|---|---|
| SAINT, Chaccour, Spain 2021 [W3111068209] | **Include** | Double-blind pilot; 12 vs 12 outpatients; single 400 µg/kg dose vs placebo; registered (NCT04390022) | PCR-positive on day 7: RR 0.92 (0.77–1.09). Lower viral load and IgG, not significant. Faster recovery of smell (76 vs 158 patient-days, p < 0.001). Very small |
| COVER, Buonfrate, Italy 2022 [W4212946211] | **Include** (3 arms: 600 and 1200 µg/kg vs placebo) | Double-blind dose-finding; 93 randomised; no or few symptoms; stopped early because cases dropped | No serious drug reactions. Fall in viral load 2.9 / 2.5 / 2.0 log units; not significant (p = 0.099 and 0.122). Pre-specify how you'll handle two ivermectin arms sharing one placebo group |
| Krolewiecki, Argentina 2021 [W3170319714] | **Include** | Outcome assessors blinded; 30 vs 15 hospitalised patients; 600 µg/kg/day × 5 days + standard care vs standard care | No difference in viral-load reduction between the groups. A difference appeared only among patients with higher ivermectin blood levels, which is not a randomised comparison. No clinical differences at days 7 and 30 |
| IVERCOR-COVID19, Vallejos, Argentina 2021 [W3173645873] | **Include** | Double-blind; 250 vs 251 outpatients; placebo | Hospitalisation 5.6% vs 8.4%, OR 0.65 (0.32–1.31), not significant. Patients on ivermectin needed mechanical ventilation **sooner** (5.25 vs 10 days, p = 0.019). PCR results and safety no different |
| de la Rocha, Mexico 2022 [W4311938754] | **Include** | Double-blind; 66 patients with no or mild symptoms; ivermectin + paracetamol vs placebo + paracetamol, so both arms got paracetamol; registered | No one got severe in either group. Symptoms similar. Viral load differed on day 5 only (p = 0.039). One serious adverse event in the ivermectin arm |
| Ochoa-Jaramillo, Colombia 2022 [W4307216937] | **Include** | Double-blind; 37 vs 38 hospitalised with severe COVID-19; single 400 µg/kg dose + standard care vs placebo; stopped early | ICU 21.6% vs 15.8% (difference 5.8 points, −11.8 to 23.5). Mechanical ventilation 18.9% vs 13.2%. Deaths 5.4% vs 10.5% (2/37 vs 4/38). Other illnesses more common in the placebo group (78.9% vs 56.8%) |
| Ahmed, Bangladesh 2020 [W3107056972] | **Include only the ivermectin-alone vs placebo comparison** | Double-blind, 3 arms; 72 **hospitalised** patients with mild disease | Viral clearance 9.7 vs 12.7 days (p = 0.02). Symptoms similar across groups. No serious adverse events. The ivermectin + doxycycline arm is out under the same-other-treatments rule. I had listed this trial with the outpatient group; move it to the hospitalised group |

## Updated totals
- **Included: 33 trials in 32 papers.** That's the 26 from before plus these 7. The Rezai paper still counts as two trials.
- **Still pending: Shakhsi Niaee [W3111064783].** The question is still whether the ivermectin arms also got hydroxychloroquine like the control arms. You didn't ask me to open it, but it's the last unresolved decision.
- **Add to the excluded list:** Rani [W3213437465] (duplicate data, not an original trial), Helaly [W4220764004] (review), Sekhon [W4289979425] (observational).

## Effect on the synthesis
None of the new trials changes the conclusions, but they add some data:
- **Hospitalisation:** IVERCOR is the third-largest outpatient trial with this outcome. Its OR of 0.65 (0.32–1.31) leans toward benefit but includes no effect, much like TOGETHER (RR 0.90). The Colombian trial in severe disease leans toward harm for ICU admission. The Mexico trial had no events.
- **Deaths:** the Colombian trial adds another small, imprecise result favouring ivermectin (2 vs 4 deaths). It fits the existing pattern: small trials with few events and confidence intervals that include no effect.
- **Symptoms:** Ahmed and the Mexico trial found no symptom difference. SAINT's faster recovery of smell is one secondary outcome in 24 patients.
- **Viral load:** Ahmed, the Mexico trial (day 5 only) and Krolewiecki (patients with high drug levels only) report some antiviral effect. SAINT, COVER and IVERCOR don't. None of these effects comes with a clinical benefit.
